source: Liu et al. (2021) What Makes Good In-Context Examples for GPT-3? (KATE)
finding: Picking the nearest neighbours of the test input as GPT-3 demonstrations beats random demonstrations. Random demos give large variance. Encoders fine-tuned on a related task retrieve better.
numbers: SST-2 five random demo sets: 94.6/95.0/95.8/93.9/86.9 accuracy. NQ, 100 test questions: closest-10 neighbours EM 46.0 vs farthest-10 EM 31.0. IMDB with SST-2 demos: random 87.95 +-2.74, KATE-roberta 91.99, KATE fine-tuned on SST-2 93.43. NQ EM: random 28.6, KATE-nli+sts-b about 41 to 42 (abstract: 45.5 on NQ). ToTTo BLEU: random 28.4 vs KATE-roberta 40.3.
limits: GPT-3 (2021) only. Fine-tuning the encoder on a dissimilar task (NLI, STS-B) slightly hurt IMDB and ToTTo. Best demo order was data-dependent (reverse order better on NQ, default slightly better on WQ and TriviaQA).
agent_relevance: Similarity retrieval of past cases is a large, cheap win over random cases, and the farthest cases are much worse than the nearest. The similarity metric must match the task.

source: Liu et al. (2021) KATE, kNN-only control
finding: Control: using the nearest neighbours' labels directly (kNN, no LLM) is far worse than letting GPT-3 read them. Retrieval and the LM work together.
numbers: IMDB: kNN on RoBERTa embeddings about 50.2 accuracy (near chance) vs KATE 91.99. ToTTo BLEU: kNN 14.1 vs random 28.4 vs KATE 40.3. NQ with 64 neighbours by majority vote: EM about the same as top-1 kNN.
limits: Same paper, same limits.
agent_relevance: Case retrieval is not the answer by itself. The model adapts the retrieved cases, so retrieval quality and reuse must be tested together (guardrail G7: pay for itself at equal tokens).

source: Rubin, Herzig, Berant (2022) Learning To Retrieve Prompts for In-Context Learning (EPR)
finding: Train a dense retriever with labels from the LM itself (probability of the gold output given a candidate demo). This beats surface similarity (BM25, SBERT) and even BM25 run on the gold output.
numbers: Dev results (BREAK LF-EM / MTOP EM / SMCalFlow EM), GPT-Neo 2.7B: Random 1.7/7.3/8.9; SBERT 21.6/48.7/43.6; BM25 26.0/52.9/46.1; CBR retriever 25.7/57.0/51.4; EPR 31.9/64.2/54.3; BM25-oracle 32.3/58.9/47.3; LM-oracle 43.1/71.6/73.7. Test: BREAK NEM BM25 17.6, EPR 23.9; MTOP BM25 49.0, EPR 64.4.
limits: Structured semantic parsing tasks with 3 datasets; small LMs (GPT-Neo, GPT-J) mostly; GPT-3 and Codex as inference LMs only in proxy mode. Needs labelled training data and LM scoring passes.
agent_relevance: Surface similarity is a weak proxy. A learned score of whether this case helped the model solve the target is stronger (+6 to +8 points over the best unsupervised baseline on MTOP and BREAK). Our agent can log which retrieved cases helped and learn a usefulness score.

source: Rubin et al. (2022) EPR, copying analysis and proxy-LM transfer
finding: A small LM can train the retriever for a larger LM. The inference LM copies patterns mostly from the top-ranked retrieved prompts.
numbers: Proxy: GPT-Neo-trained retriever gives 2 to 8 points over BM25 and CBR on GPT-J, GPT-3, Codex. GPT-J on BREAK: 31.5 (Neo-trained) vs 33.6 (GPT-J-trained). Codex: 29.5 vs 29.3. MTOP: 84.5 percent of examples abstractly copied; accuracy on copied subset 71.6 EM vs 64.2 on all. One-shot BREAK: EPR beats best baseline by 8.5 and BM25-oracle by 5; ANYCORRECT-oracle (any BM25 candidate works) reaches 53.6, 20 points above LM-oracle.
limits: Copying rate is much lower on BREAK than MTOP/SMCalFlow. Non-copied cases still have non-zero accuracy, so the model generalises somewhat beyond the cases.
agent_relevance: Rank order matters: the top cases are the ones the model copies. The big gap between LM-oracle and EPR says retrieval is still far from solved even with a learned scorer.

source: Ye et al. (2023) Compositional Exemplars for In-context Learning (CEIL)
finding: Choose the whole SET of demos with a conditional determinantal point process (relevance times diversity), trained with LM feedback. Beats top-k and EPR on 12 datasets.
numbers: 12 datasets, 7 tasks. Over learning-free retrievers: more than 20 points absolute on NLI (QNLI, MNLI), about 10 points on most others; smaller gain on commonsense (CMSQA, HellaSwag). Generation tasks benefit more than classification. Retrieving 50 demos: top-k 30 s vs DPP-MAP 36 s on SST5 (1.2x). Retriever trained on GPT-Neo transfers to GPT2-XL and Codex.
limits: One-stage random subset retrieval had the LOWEST MRR yet some subsets still worked, so relevance is not the only factor in a good set. Validation-set results only.
agent_relevance: Pick a set of cases that jointly covers the problem, not the k independent nearest ones. In code this is a cheap re-ranking step (G5: code selects).

source: Levy, Bogin, Berant (2023) Diverse Demonstrations Improve In-context Compositional Generalization
finding: When no single stored case is close enough, similarity-only top-k returns near-duplicates. Selecting demos that cover the needed output structures (or are mutually dissimilar) fixes this.
numbers: Up to 23 absolute points over similarity-only retrieval, e.g. SMCalFlow-CS 50.3 -> 73.5. Diversity methods (Cover-Utt, DPP, Cover-LS) beat Top-K in 7 of 8 compositional splits without fine-tuning, and beat an ORACLE Top-K that sees the gold program.
limits: Semantic parsing with formal programs and BM25 or SBERT retrievers; benefits are for compositional splits, not i.i.d. splits where plain similarity works well.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for nearest-case retrieval: on novel problems, coverage of sub-parts beats global nearness. This links to decomposition: retrieve per sub-goal, not per whole task.

source: Min et al. (2022) Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations: What Makes In-Context Learning Work?
finding: Replacing the labels in demonstrations with random labels barely hurts in-context learning. The input distribution, label space and format of the demos matter more than correct input-label pairs.
numbers: k=16 demos, 5 seeds; 12 models incl. GPT-3, MetaICL, GPT-J; 16 classification + 10 multi-choice datasets. Random labels cost 0.8 to 1.6 points across k; MetaICL only 0.1 to 0.9 absolute. Demos preserve 92 / 100 / 97 percent of the gain in MetaICL classification / MetaICL multi-choice / GPT-J multi-choice. One setting (GPT-J classification, many incorrect labels) saw nearly a 10 percent drop.
limits: Random (not retrieved) demos and mostly small or mid models. With retrieved near-duplicate inputs the model can copy the label, so label correctness may matter more (see EPR copying analysis).
agent_relevance: What a retrieved case supplies may be format and domain more than the answer. Do not trust a retrieved solution as true; G3 and G2 apply (check on held-out or real output).

source: Agarwal et al. (2024) Many-Shot In-Context Learning
finding: With very long contexts, many examples beat few. Gains continue to hundreds of shots on some tasks and can override pretraining bias. One task degrades at 250 shots.
numbers: Low-resource translation: many-shot over 1-shot gains 15.3 percent on Bemba and 4.5 percent on Kurdish. On one task 125-shot with ground-truth rationales nearly matches Claude-3 Opus, then performance degrades at 250 shots. Flipped and abstract labels approach default-label accuracy as shots grow.
limits: Gemini 1.5 Pro with 1M context; no retrieval, examples fixed. I read selected passages, not all tables.
agent_relevance: Competing strategy to nearest-case retrieval: when context is cheap, include many cases. Memento and ReasoningBank find the opposite for agent cases (small K best), so cases and demonstrations behave differently.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM Agents without Fine-tuning LLMs
finding: A deep-research agent keeps a case bank of (task, plan, success) triples and retrieves by encoder similarity, or by a learned Q-function that estimates whether a case is a good reference. Both help, learned selection helps slightly more.
numbers: GAIA validation 87.88 percent Pass@3, test 79.40 percent. DeepResearcher 7-dataset result F1 66.6 / PM 80.4 (abstract). Case memory adds +4.7 to +9.6 absolute points on out-of-distribution sets. Learning curve over 5 iterations (accuracy): no CBR 78.65 -> 84.47; non-parametric CBR 79.84 -> 84.85; parametric Q-function CBR 80.46 -> 85.44.
limits: Self-reported on a closed dataset of about 3k training items; case bank saturates quickly; GPT-4.1 planner with o3 or o4-mini executors; non-parametric retrieval uses SimCSE cosine; single paper, no independent replication.
agent_relevance: Direct template for our agent: store (task, plan, outcome) with outcome label, retrieve by cosine, optionally learn a utility score. Gains over no-CBR are small after convergence (0.4 to 1.0 points at iteration 5).

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento, number of retrieved cases K
finding: Retrieving more cases does not keep helping. Best K is 4; more cases add noise. The authors contrast this with few-shot prompting where more examples often help.
numbers: DeepResearcher avg F1/PM by K: K=0 59.9/72.2; K=1 63.6/77.9; K=2 63.7/78.1; K=4 64.5/78.5; K=8 64.1/78.2; K=16 63.9/78.1; K=32 63.9/78.1. Most of the gain (about 3.7 F1) comes from the first case.
quote: CBR benefits from a small, high-quality memory, unlike few-shot prompting, where more examples often help
limits: Differences between K=2 and K=32 are under 1 point and no variance is reported, so only the jump from 0 to 1 is clearly real.
agent_relevance: Default to 1 to 4 retrieved cases. A cap on retrieved cases is cheap and costs nothing in this evidence.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory
finding: Agent stores distilled strategy items (title, description, content) from self-judged successes AND failures, retrieved by embedding cosine of the task query. Beats raw-trajectory memory and success-only workflow memory.
numbers: WebArena success rate gains over memory-free agent: +8.3, +7.2, +4.6 for three backbones. WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash: Synapse (raw successful trajectories) 40.6 -> 41.7 when failures are added; ReasoningBank gains more. Retrieval: gemini-embedding-001, cosine, default top-1.
limits: Authors' own comparison (author list not verified by me); the retrieval pipeline is deliberately simple, so the gain is from what is stored, not from better similarity. Self-judged outcome labels (no ground truth) may be noisy.
agent_relevance: What is indexed matters more than the similarity function: abstracted strategies beat raw trajectories. Failure cases need labelling to be useful.

source: ReasoningBank (2025), number of retrieved experiences
finding: More retrieved experiences lowered success rate. One was best.
numbers: WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash success rate: k=1 49.7; k=2 46.0; k=3 45.5; k=4 44.4.
quote: the relevance and quality of memory are more crucial than sheer quantity
limits: Text extracted from a two-column figure and partly garbled; the k=2 value (46.0) is my reading. One backbone, one site.
agent_relevance: Matches Memento's saturation. Evidence from two agent papers that one to four cases is the working range.

source: Zhao et al. (2023) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners
finding: Agent retrieves past successful trajectories by task-text similarity (all-mpnet-base-v2, Faiss kNN) and also uses extracted insights. Task-similarity retrieval beats both random cases and reasoning-step similarity.
numbers: ALFWorld success rate (ablation): ReAct 40.0 +-0.3; reasoning-step-similarity retrieval 48.5 +-2.1; random successful trajectories 42.5 +-0.8; task-similarity ExpeL 59.0 +-0.3. Insights-only vs retrieval-only: HotpotQA 36/31, ALFWorld 50/55 percent. Transfer HotpotQA insights to FEVER: Act 58, ReAct 63, ExpeL without task demos 65, ExpeL 70.
limits: GPT-3.5/GPT-4 era agent, three text environments, few seeds. Reason-similarity re-retrieval each step changes few-shot cases mid-trajectory, which the authors say causes instability.
agent_relevance: Random cases barely help (+2.5 points) while task-similar cases help a lot (+19). Retrieve once per task by task description, not every step. Retrieved cases help embodied/procedural tasks; abstract insights help knowledge tasks.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Instead of retrieving whole past examples (the Synapse approach), induce reusable abstract workflows from past tasks and give those. Less bias toward copying element choices from concrete examples.
numbers: Relative success rate +24.6 percent on Mind2Web and +51.1 percent on WebArena. Versus Synapse (retrieves the most relevant training examples): +5.0 element accuracy and +4.0 step success rate on Mind2Web. Gains grow with train-test gap: 8.9 to 14.0 absolute points over baselines.
limits: Web navigation only; workflows induced by an LLM, so errors in induction can propagate; text-only agent.
agent_relevance: Competing evidence: abstracted cases generalise better than nearest concrete cases when tasks shift. Our retrieval should be able to return abstractions, not only raw cases.

source: Wiratunga et al. (2024) CBR-RAG: Case-Based Reasoning for Retrieval Augmented Generation in LLMs for Legal Question Answering
finding: Treat QA pairs plus supporting text plus extracted entities as cases. Compare intra-embeddings (question to question) and inter-embeddings (question to any part), and hybrid weights. Hybrid AnglE-BERT retrieval with 3 neighbours and full cases gave the best answers.
numbers: Case base: 2,124 LLM-generated QA pairs (Australian Open Legal QA), 32 test cases. Mistral-7B answer cosine to reference: No-RAG 0.8967; Hybrid AnglEBERT k=3 full case 0.9141 (about +1.94 percent). Hybrid BERT k=1 full case 0.9068; LegalBERT k=3 0.9045. One-tailed t-test: AnglEBERT k=3 beats No-RAG and LegalBERT k=3 at 95 percent, BERT k=1 at 90 percent. Best retrieval weights [0.25,0.40,0.35] (question, support, entities).
limits: Tiny test set (32), synthetic questions made by an LLM, metric is embedding cosine to a reference (not correctness), no expert evaluation. Baseline cosine already near 0.90. Domain-specific LegalBERT did NOT win.
agent_relevance: A case-structure idea: weighted similarity over several slots (task, support, entities). Evidence quality is weak; treat the effect size as unproven.

source: Wang et al. (2024) DS-Agent: Automated Data Science by Empowering LLMs with Case-Based Reasoning
finding: Full CBR loop for data science tasks: retrieve Kaggle-derived cases by cosine of task-description embeddings, re-rank them with an LLM using the last execution feedback (ReviseRank), reuse, revise. Simplified one-shot retrieve-adapt in deployment.
numbers: Development stage with GPT-4: 100 percent success on 12 tasks. Deployment: 85 percent (GPT-3.5) and 99 percent (GPT-4) one-pass rate on 18 tasks; 36 percent average one-pass improvement across LLMs. Ablation, average best rank (lower is better): DS-Agent 2.08; without ReviseRank 2.58; without CBR 3.41. Cost 1.60 and 0.13 USD per run (GPT-4). Deployment baselines include one random case.
limits: 30 tasks total, authors' own benchmark, cases curated from Kaggle experts. Rank metric with small N. Author list not verified by me.
agent_relevance: Evidence that re-ranking retrieved cases on real execution feedback helps (rank 2.58 -> 2.08). This fits G2 (revise from real output): the feedback, not the model's opinion, steers retrieval.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
finding: Memory retrieval score = recency + importance + relevance (embedding cosine to the current query), each min-max scaled, equal weights of 1. Top memories that fit in context go in the prompt.
numbers: Believability TrueSkill (100 human rankers): full architecture mu=29.89 (sigma 0.72); no reflection 26.88; no reflection or planning 25.64; human crowdworker baseline 22.95; no observation/planning/reflection lowest.
limits: Ablations remove whole memory types, not the retrieval terms, so the three retrieval weights are not individually tested. Authors report retrieval failures: wrong or incomplete memory fragments retrieved. Short two-day simulation.
agent_relevance: Multi-factor retrieval (recency, importance, similarity) is a known design; ablating each term is untested here, so for us it is a [D] placeholder.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
finding: A skill library of verified code programs is indexed by an embedding of an LLM-written description. Retrieval queries with the embedding of the self-generated plan plus environment feedback, and returns the top-5 skills.
numbers: Versus ReAct, Reflexion, AutoGPT: 3.3x more unique items, tech-tree milestones up to 15.3x faster, 2.3x longer distances. Skills are only added after verification by running the code.
limits: Minecraft with GPT-4; the gain combines curriculum, skills and iterative prompting, so retrieval quality is not isolated by the abstract-level numbers I recorded.
agent_relevance: Two good patterns: index by a description of what the case does, and add a case to memory only after it passes a check (G3).

source: Liu et al. (2023) Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
finding: When retrieved documents are put into the prompt, models use the first and last ones best and the middle worst (U-shaped curve), even for long-context models.
numbers: Multi-document QA with 10, 20, 30 documents. GPT-3.5-Turbo accuracy can drop by more than 20 percent from best to worst position; closed-book baseline is 56.1 percent and the paper reports multi-document performance with the answer mid-context at or below that level. U-shape appears for large Llama-2 only (7B variants flatter); instruction tuning is not the cause (MPT-30B base also U-shaped).
limits: Models of 2023. Newer long-context models may differ. I did not verify the exact mid-position figure against the closed-book line.
agent_relevance: Order retrieved cases so the best-matching ones are at the start or the end of the prompt, and keep the count small.

source: Cuconasu et al. (2024) The Power of Noise: Redefining Retrieval for RAG Systems
finding: Highly-scored retrieved documents that do not contain the answer (distractors) hurt. Surprisingly, unrelated random documents added to the prompt can raise accuracy.
numbers: NQ-open, 10K training queries, gold document placed near the query. Random documents improve accuracy by up to 35 percent (abstract); +0.08 (+36 percent) in the best near setting. Llama2 with 18 distracting docs: accuracy 0.37, 0.23, 0.17 for the three gold-document positions (best when the gold is near the query).
limits: Open-domain QA with a few 7B-class LLMs; mechanism unclear. Not a CBR task. Position labels for the 0.37/0.23/0.17 triple are inferred as near/middle/far.
agent_relevance: Warning: near-miss cases (similar but wrong) are the harmful kind. Similarity alone cannot tell a helpful case from a distracting one, so a check on usefulness is needed.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context (GSM-IC)
finding: Adding one irrelevant sentence to grade-school math problems sharply reduces accuracy for all prompting methods. An instruction to ignore irrelevant text and self-consistency reduce the damage.
numbers: GSM-IC-4K (4,000 problems); among base problems solved by greedy decoding, no more than 18 percent are solved for all irrelevant-information types. Self-consistency with 20 samples adds more than 11 points of micro accuracy and recall of the correct answer reaches 99.7 percent. Irrelevant context in exemplars or an instruction to ignore it raises accuracy; no drop on clean GSM8K.
limits: code-davinci-002 and text-davinci-003; math only. Irrelevant info was synthetic.
agent_relevance: A retrieved case that is topically close but not applicable acts as irrelevant context. Tell the model retrieved cases may not apply and make it check applicability.

source: Steck, Ekanadham, Kallus (2024) Is Cosine-Similarity of Embeddings Really About Similarity?
finding: For embeddings learned with regularised linear models, cosine similarity can give arbitrary results because the learned vectors are only defined up to a rescaling that cosine does not ignore.
numbers: Analytic result, shown for two L2-regularisation schemes in matrix factorisation; illustrated with simulated data. No LLM benchmark numbers.
limits: Theory for linear models; extension to deep encoders such as those used in KATE or CBR-RAG is by analogy only.
agent_relevance: Cosine over off-the-shelf embeddings is the default similarity in nearly every agent memory paper above; it is a convenience, not a validated measure of case usefulness.

source: Xiao et al. (2025) BRIGHT: A Realistic and Challenging Benchmark for Reasoning-Intensive Retrieval
finding: When relevance needs reasoning (same theory, same algorithm, different surface), standard embedding retrievers fail. Rewriting the query with explicit reasoning helps.
numbers: 1,384 queries across economics, psychology, maths, coding. Best MTEB retriever (SFR-Embedding-Mistral, 59.0 nDCG@10 on MTEB) gets only 18.3 nDCG@10 on BRIGHT. Reasoning about the query improves retrieval up to 12.2 points. 13 retrieval models evaluated.
limits: Document-retrieval setting; relevance labels built by annotators and may not equal usefulness to a specific solver. First-author attribution not verified by me.
agent_relevance: Core problem for case-based thinking: structural similarity (the case that solves it the same way) is not surface similarity. Retrieve on a reasoned description of the problem, not the raw text.

source: Cross-paper synthesis: surface vs structure
finding: Four lines point the same way. Nearest-neighbour by surface similarity beats random (KATE, ExpeL). Learned or LM-scored usefulness beats surface similarity (EPR). Diverse or set-level selection beats top-k on novel problems (CEIL, Levy). Reasoned query description beats raw text on structural tasks (BRIGHT).
numbers: EPR over the best baseline on each set: +5.9 BREAK (vs BM25 26.0), +7.2 MTOP (vs CBR retriever 57.0), +2.9 SMCalFlow (vs CBR retriever 51.4); Levy +23 points on SMCalFlow-CS; BRIGHT 59.0 to 18.3 nDCG; ExpeL random 42.5 vs task-similar 59.0.
limits: Different tasks, models and metrics; no common benchmark compares all four selection ideas head to head on one LLM agent task.
agent_relevance: A sensible retrieval stack for the agent: cheap embedding recall, code-side dedupe and coverage re-rank, a small cap (1 to 4), and logged usefulness. Test each step against plain at equal tokens (G7).

source: Cross-paper synthesis: how many cases
finding: In agent settings the best count of retrieved cases is small. In plain demonstration settings with long context it can be large.
numbers: Memento best K=4 (F1 64.5); ReasoningBank best k=1 (49.7, falling to 44.4 at k=4); Many-shot ICL keeps improving to about 125 shots on some tasks and degrades at 250 on one.
limits: Different case types: agent plans and strategies (long, specific) vs short labelled input-output pairs.
agent_relevance: Treat retrieved plans as scarce context. Set default k=1 to 3, and measure before raising it.

source: Gap note: no head-to-head LLM-era test of Weber/Richter style similarity measures found
finding: The classic CBR similarity toolkit (weighted local similarities per attribute and a global aggregate, as in Richter and Weber) appears in the LLM era only in CBR-RAG (weights on question, support, entities) and DS-Agent (cosine plus LLM re-rank). I found no paper that tests hand-built attribute similarity against plain embeddings on an LLM agent task with matched budgets.
numbers: CBR-RAG: weights [0.25, 0.40, 0.35] best on retrieval F1 over a 32-case test; effect on answers +1.94 percent cosine. No other paired test found in this session.
limits: Search tools were rate-limited (WebSearch budget exhausted; arXiv search, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs returned 429), so the gap claim rests on the papers opened, not an exhaustive search. Treat as unverified. The classic Weber/Richter papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: A cheap own experiment: attribute-weighted similarity vs embedding cosine on our own case store, same tokens, report both.
